description.text: Agnes of Rome was a Roman Christian adolescent who was martyred during the Diocletian persecution. Born into Roman nobility around 291, she was raised as a Christian and refused to renounce her faith, leading to her execution at the age of 12 or 13 on 21 January 304.

Her martyrdom is recorded by the 4th‑century theologian St Ambrose and later traditions. Agnes is venerated as a virgin martyr, with iconography that includes a lamb, a sword, and a palm branch. Her relics are preserved in Rome: her skull is kept in a chapel of Sant’Agnese in Agone, while her bones lie beneath the altar of Sant’Agnese fuori le mura.

curiosities.text: Legend says that while Agnes prayed, her hair grew to cover her body and men who tried to assault her were immediately blinded.
Her foster‑sister Emerentiana was stoned to death a few days after Agnes’s burial for praying at her tomb.
Since the 16th century, the tradition of blessing lambs on Saint Agnes’s feast day has been practiced, with lambs from the Trappist abbey of Tre Fontane in Rome.
Agnes’s skull is preserved in a separate chapel of Sant’Agnese in Agone, while her bones are conserved beneath the high altar of the church built over her tomb in Rome.
